title: Late wage board fuelled garment unrest, says CPD's Nazneen Ahmed
excerpt: CPD's executive director says wages should be set on time, using living-cost data, before protests start.

image.alt: A production hall inside a Bangladeshi garment factory

content:
Garment unrest could have been avoided if the minimum wage board had been formed before workers began protesting, Dr Nazneen Ahmed, executive director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said in Dhaka on Friday, 13 November, The Business Standard reported.

She was chief guest at a debate organised by Debate for Democracy on whether safe working conditions and social security matter more than wage rises for stability in the garment sector.

What she said

A new wage board was due in 2026, three years after the last one in 2023, but the government formed it only after protests began, Dr Ahmed said. "It is not desirable to take initiatives to increase workers' wages after an unstable situation has emerged," she said.

She said neither side is satisfied. Workers are unhappy with pay and conditions, while factory owners face energy shortages, port problems and low productivity.

Her recommendations

  • Set the minimum wage using inflation, living costs and workers' spending on education and health.
  • Have the government collect living-cost data from a large share of the population.
  • Take factory owners' ability to pay into account.

Hasan Ahmed Chowdhury Kiran, chairman of Debate for Democracy, said the situation had improved after weeks of protests and road blockades over workers' five-point demands, but stability had not fully returned. He warned that the unrest could cost buyers' confidence and exports.

Why it matters

The wage board has agreed that new wages will start in December, and owners are considering closing 210 factories in Ashulia under Section 13 of the labour law. Labour rights NGOs, legal aid groups and programmes for garment workers' health and childcare should expect more demand while the wage is negotiated. Brands and donors funding supply-chain work will watch whether wage setting becomes regular and evidence-based, as CPD proposes.

What to watch

The wage board's next meeting and figures from owners and workers, and whether factories in Ashulia reopen or close under Section 13.
